title: Water Off a Duck's Back
blurb: The bird that sits on freezing water all day, stays bone dry, and sleeps with half its brain awake.

blocks.prompt: The Duck's Little Bottle of Oil
blocks.text: A duck has a secret. Near her tail there is a tiny bump. The bump makes oil. The duck rubs her bill on the bump. Then she pushes the oil through her feathers, one at a time. This is called preening. The oil makes her feathers slick, so water rolls off and never soaks in. Under those feathers is soft down. The down holds warm air close to her skin. That is why a duck can sit on cold water all day and stay warm and dry. A duckling learns to preen by watching its mom do it.

3.title: Water Off a Duck's Back
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Ducks can stand on ice without cold hurting them

blocks.prompt: Why a Duck Can Stand on Ice
blocks.text: Put your bare foot on an ice cube and it hurts in seconds. A duck can stand on a frozen pond all morning and not seem to notice. Here is how that works. A duck's feet are mostly bone, skin, and tough cords called tendons. There is very little muscle down there and hardly any nerve to feel the ache. But the real trick is in the blood. The warm blood heading down into the foot runs right alongside the cool blood coming back up. The two flow in opposite directions, close enough to trade heat. The warm blood hands its heat to the cool blood before it ever reaches the toes. So the heat turns around and goes back into the duck. The duck's feet stay cold. That sounds bad, but it is exactly right. Cold feet lose almost no heat to the ice. A warm foot would pour heat straight into the frozen pond all day. Instead the duck keeps its warmth where it is needed, and walks across the ice like it is nothing at all.

4.title: Water Off a Duck's Back
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: What a Duck's Bill Can Really Do
blocks.text: A duck's bill looks like a simple orange shovel. It is closer to a tool kit. Run a finger along the inside edge of a duck's bill and you would feel a row of fine ridges called lamellae. They work like the teeth of a comb. A mallard tips forward, takes in a mouthful of pond, and pumps the water back out through those ridges. Seeds, snails, and insects are too big to fit through the gaps, so they stay behind. The duck swallows the food and lets the water go. It is a strainer built into a face. The bill can also feel. Packed into the tip are thousands of tiny touch sensors, so densely that the end of the bill works something like your fingertips. This matters more than it sounds. A duck often feeds in water so muddy it cannot see its own feet. It does not need to see. It sweeps the bill through the muck and feels the difference between a pebble and a snail, then keeps one and drops the other. Not every duck feeds the same way. Dabbling ducks, like mallards, stay at the surface and tip up with their tails in the air, reaching down with their necks. Diving ducks push under completely and swim to the bottom to work. Same tool, two very different jobs. The next time you see a row of duck tails pointing at the sky, you are watching a whole line of strainers at work underneath.

5.title: Water Off a Duck's Back
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ducklings hatch with their eyes already open
Precocial: born far along and ready to go
Imprinting locks a duckling onto the first mover

The ducklings jump the next morning and bounce
Konrad Lorenz had to quack to be followed

blocks.prompt: Born Ready
blocks.text: Most baby birds are hopeless at first. A robin hatches naked, blind, and helpless. It lies in the nest with its mouth open for two weeks while its parents work themselves ragged hauling in food. A duckling hatches ready to go. Its eyes are already open. It arrives wearing a coat of warm down. Within a day it can walk, swim, and find its own food. Biologists call this precocial, which simply means born far along. The mother duck never feeds her ducklings. She leads them, warms them, and watches for danger. They handle the rest themselves. Being born ready comes with a problem attached. A duckling that can walk away on its first day can also walk away from the wrong bird, or follow one. So ducklings are built to lock on fast. In their first hours, the first large moving thing that makes roughly the right noise becomes mom, permanently. The word for this is imprinting. It usually works, because the first large moving thing in a duckling's life is almost always its actual mother. When Konrad Lorenz raised mallard ducklings in the 1930s, they followed him instead, but he found they would only do it if he crouched down low and quacked as he walked. Standing up and staying quiet was enough to break the spell. Wood ducks push the whole idea to its limit. They nest inside tree holes, sometimes fifty feet above the ground. The morning after they hatch, the mother drops to the ground below and calls up. The ducklings scramble to the entrance, look out at nothing, and jump. They weigh almost nothing and they are essentially a ball of down, so they hit the leaf litter, bounce, shake it off, and toddle after her to the water. Not one of them has ever done it before. It is a terrifying way to begin a life, and it works.

6.title: Water Off a Duck's Back
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Anatidae: roughly 120 species of duck

blocks.prompt: The Question That Sounded Silly
blocks.text: For years a rumor circulated with all the confidence of a fact: a duck's quack does not echo, and no one knows why. It turned up on lists of amazing facts and got repeated at dinner tables for decades. The claim has two qualities that kept it alive. It sounds specific enough to be true, and the little tag on the end, and no one knows why, quietly discourages you from asking. If nobody knows, why would you check. In 2003 an acoustics engineer named Trevor Cox, at the University of Salford, decided to just check. He borrowed a duck named Daisy and recorded her in two rooms built for exactly this kind of question. The first was an anechoic chamber, a room lined with deep foam wedges that swallow sound so completely it is among the quietest places on Earth. The second was a reverberation chamber, all hard reflective surfaces, where a sound bounces around for a long time before it dies. Daisy quacked in both rooms. The recordings were not the same. In the reverberation chamber the quack echoed, plainly and obviously. The rumor was simply false. The interesting part is the explanation, because the rumor did grow out of something real. A quack is not a sharp bark. It begins loud and then trails off, fading gradually into silence. An echo comes back a fraction of a second later, and it arrives while the original quack is still fading away. The soft returning echo lands underneath the sound that produced it, and your ear folds the two together and reads the whole thing as one long quack. Sound engineers call this masking. On top of that, ducks spend their lives on ponds, marshes, and open fields, where there is usually no hard surface anywhere nearby to bounce a sound back. People who believed quacks do not echo had mostly just never heard one in the right room. Ducks reward this kind of checking. Consider another claim that sounds invented: a duck can sleep with half of its brain. In 1999 a team led by Niels Rattenborg tested it by lining four mallards up in a row and filming them while recording their brain activity. The two birds on the ends slept with the outward-facing eye open far more often than the birds tucked safely in the middle, and the recordings showed the matching half of the brain staying awake while the other half slept. Turn the row around, and the end birds switched which eye they kept open. The duck on the edge is the one that gets eaten, so the duck on the edge keeps watch with half of itself. Two odd claims, both testable. One survived and one collapsed. The difference was never how strange the claim sounded. It was whether anyone was willing to put a duck in a room and find out.
